title: Architecture of the CPU
summary: The CPU is the part of the computer that actually runs your program. This topic covers what it does (the fetch–decode–execute cycle), the components that do it, the registers Von Neumann architecture uses, and the stored program concept. It comes up on almost every Paper 1, and the 6-mark "describe how the registers are used" question is worth drilling until it is automatic.

blocks.text: The CPU (Central Processing Unit) is the processor. Its job is to fetch instructions from memory, work out what they mean, and carry them out. Everything a computer does comes down to this one loop repeating billions of times a second.
That loop is called the fetch–decode–execute cycle, and it never stops while the computer is on.

steps.title: Fetch
steps.text: The address in the program counter is copied to the MAR. The instruction at that address is fetched from memory into the MDR. The program counter is then incremented so it points at the next instruction.

steps.title: Decode
steps.text: The control unit examines the instruction and works out what operation is required and what data it needs.

steps.title: Execute
steps.text: The instruction is carried out. If it involves a calculation or comparison, the ALU does the work and the result is placed in the accumulator.

blocks.caption: One cycle, end to end. The program counter is incremented as soon as its address reaches the MAR — long before the instruction has finished executing.

blocks.title: What earns the marks
blocks.text: A three-mark "describe the cycle" question wants one clear point per stage. If the question is worth more, name the registers involved in each stage — that is where the extra marks live.

rows: Performs all arithmetic (add, subtract, multiply) and all logic operations (AND, OR, NOT, and comparisons like "is x greater than y?")
Decodes each instruction and sends control signals telling the other components what to do and when
Very fast memory very close to the CPU, holding frequently used instructions and data so the CPU does not have to wait for RAM
Tiny, extremely fast storage locations inside the CPU that hold the values being worked on right now

blocks.title: The speed hierarchy
blocks.text: Registers are fastest, then cache, then RAM, then secondary storage. Each step down is roughly an order of magnitude slower. Almost every performance question in this unit comes back to keeping data as high up that list as possible.

sections.title: Von Neumann architecture and its registers

blocks.text: Von Neumann architecture is the design nearly all modern computers use. Its defining feature is that instructions and data are stored together in the same memory, and the program is held in memory rather than being hard-wired into the machine. That is why one computer can run any program.

blocks.caption: The four Von Neumann registers and how data moves between the CPU and memory.

rows: The memory address of the next instruction to be fetched
The address of the memory location currently being read from or written to
The actual data or instruction that has just been fetched, or is about to be written
The result of a calculation performed by the ALU

blocks.title: MAR and MDR get mixed up constantly
blocks.text: MAR holds the address — where. MDR holds the data — what. If you can remember that "A is for Address", you will not lose these marks.

This is the phrase the exam asks for by name, and it is worth learning as a sentence rather than as a vague idea. The stored program concept means that the program’s instructions AND the data those instructions work on are held together in the same main memory, and are fetched from there one at a time to be executed.

Before Von Neumann, a machine had to be physically rewired to make it do something different. Because the program is now just numbers in memory, the same computer can run any program — you load a different set of numbers. That is the whole reason a general-purpose computer exists.

blocks.title: The two-mark version
blocks.text: Instructions and data are stored in the same memory (1). The program is held in memory and its instructions are fetched and executed one at a time, rather than the machine being hard-wired (1). Both halves are needed — answers that only say "they are stored together" usually get one of the two.

sections.title: How does the CPU know an address holds an instruction and not data?

blocks.text: It cannot tell by looking. A value in memory is just a binary pattern — nothing about it says "I am an instruction". This is the price you pay for the stored program concept.

The CPU knows because of where it is in the cycle. Whatever is fetched at the address held in the program counter during the FETCH stage is treated as an instruction. Whatever that instruction then asks the CPU to go and get is treated as data. The program counter starts at the address of the first instruction, and correct execution keeps it pointing at instructions from then on.

blocks.title: What happens when it goes wrong
blocks.text: If the program counter ever ends up pointing at data, the CPU will happily try to execute that data as an instruction — and the program crashes. That is a good sentence to add if a question asks why this matters.

sections.title: Be the CPU: a worked trace

blocks.text: Six-mark questions on this topic are always some version of "describe how the registers are used to fetch and execute this instruction". The fastest way to be able to write one is to trace a short program by hand until the pattern is automatic.

rows: Load the value stored at <address> into the accumulator
Add the value stored at <address> to the accumulator
Subtract the value stored at <address> from the accumulator
Store the value in the accumulator at <address>

blocks.question: The program counter starts holding 100. Trace the program, giving the contents of the MAR, MDR and accumulator after each cycle, and state the value left at address 203.
steps: Cycle 1 — PC holds 100, so 100 is copied to the MAR and the PC is incremented to 101. The instruction at 100 (LDA 200) is fetched into the MDR. The CU decodes it. Executing it puts the value at address 200, which is 14, into the accumulator. ACC = 14.
Cycle 2 — PC holds 101 → MAR = 101, PC becomes 102. MDR = ADD 201. The ALU adds the value at 201 (9) to the accumulator. ACC = 23.
Cycle 3 — PC holds 102 → MAR = 102, PC becomes 103. MDR = SUB 202. The ALU subtracts the value at 202 (5). ACC = 18.
Cycle 4 — PC holds 103 → MAR = 103, PC becomes 104. MDR = STO 203. The accumulator value 18 is written to address 203. The ACC is unchanged at 18.
Cycle 5 — PC holds 104 → MAR = 104, PC becomes 105. MDR = HLT. The CPU stops.
blocks.answer: Address 203 holds 18. The ALU was used in cycles 2 and 3 only — LDA, STO and HLT move or halt, they do not calculate.

blocks.title: The rhythm of every single cycle
blocks.text: PC → MAR. PC incremented. Memory → MDR. MDR → CU to decode. Execute (ALU if needed). Result → accumulator. Say those six things in order and a 6-mark question is answered.

blocks.title: Why is the PC incremented during fetch, not at the end?
blocks.text: Because the instruction being executed may itself change the PC — a jump or a branch writes a new address into it. If the CPU incremented afterwards it would overwrite the jump and the program would go to the wrong place. Incrementing early also means the address is ready before the current instruction has finished.

sections.title: Turning what you know into marks

blocks.text: Almost nobody loses marks here because they do not know what a MAR is. They lose them by writing an answer that repeats the question back, or by giving a fact without its effect.

rows: "The CPU fetches the instruction so it can be used."
Repeats the question. Never says where the instruction comes from or how.
"The address in the program counter is copied to the MAR, and the instruction at that address is copied from memory into the MDR. The program counter is then incremented."
"The CPU is the brain of the computer."
Vague, and not what the CPU does.
A fact with no effect. "Explain" wants the consequence.
"Cache holds frequently used instructions and data, and is faster to access than RAM, so the CPU spends less time waiting and executes more instructions per second."
The CPU processes; it does not store.
"Registers and cache hold only the values in use right now. Data is stored in RAM and secondary storage."

blocks.title: Read the tariff as an instruction
blocks.text: The number of marks tells you how many separate points to make. 2 marks = two clauses. 6 marks = six distinct transfers or stages. Write a sentence, count your points, and check the number matches before moving on.

keyTerms.definition: The continuous loop in which the CPU retrieves an instruction from memory, works out what it means, and carries it out.
Arithmetic Logic Unit — carries out all arithmetic and logical operations.
Decodes instructions and coordinates the other components of the CPU.
keyTerms.examWording: decodes instructions and sends control signals

keyTerms.definition: Very fast memory close to the CPU holding frequently used data and instructions.
keyTerms.examWording: stores frequently used instructions and data so they can be accessed more quickly than from RAM

keyTerms.definition: A tiny, very fast storage location inside the CPU.
A design where instructions and data are stored together in the same memory, and programs are stored rather than hard-wired.
Program instructions and the data they use are held in the same main memory and are fetched and executed one at a time, rather than the machine being hard-wired.
keyTerms.examWording: instructions and data are stored in the same memory and fetched one at a time

keyTerms.definition: A list of instructions the CPU works through, held in memory.
A number identifying one location in memory — like a house number, not the thing inside the house.
Increase by one.
The register that temporarily holds the result of a calculation or comparison carried out by the ALU.
keyTerms.examWording: temporarily stores the result of calculations

examTips: For "describe the fetch–decode–execute cycle", give one distinct point per stage. Three stages, three marks.
If a question mentions a specific register, your answer must use that register's name — a general answer about "memory" will not do.
Most questions here are 1–4 marks, but the register walkthrough is regularly worth 6. That is the one to rehearse.
The tariff tells you how many points to make. Two marks means two separate clauses — write them, then count them.
"State the purpose of the CPU" wants "it processes instructions and data". Not "calculations", not "the brain", and not "stores data".
On a 6-mark register question, walk the cycle in order and name every register as you go: PC → MAR → memory → MDR → CU → ALU → accumulator.
commonMistakes: Swapping MAR and MDR. MAR = address, MDR = data.
Saying the cache "stores data" without saying why that matters — you need "so the CPU does not have to wait for the slower RAM".
Forgetting that the program counter is incremented during the fetch stage, not at the end of the cycle.
Writing "the CPU fetches the instruction" as a description of the fetch stage. That repeats the question — you must say where from (the address in the PC, copied via the MAR) and where to (the MDR).
Saying cache stores "recently used" data. The mark scheme wants "frequently used".
Half-answering the stored program concept. It is instructions AND data, in the SAME memory, fetched one at a time.
Saying the CPU stores the computer’s data. The CPU processes; RAM and secondary storage store.

title: Data storage
summary: Everything inside a computer is binary. This topic is how numbers, characters, images and sound all get turned into 1s and 0s — and how to do the conversions and calculations in the exam. It is the most calculation-heavy topic on Paper 1, which makes it one of the most reliable places to pick up marks.

blocks.text: Denary (base 10) is what you count in normally. Binary (base 2) is what the computer uses, because a circuit is either on or off. Hexadecimal (base 16) is a shorthand people use to write binary without going cross-eyed.

blocks.title: Learn this table
blocks.text: Sixteen rows. Every binary, hex and nibble question on the paper comes straight out of it. Ten minutes memorising this is worth more marks per minute than anything else in the unit.

blocks.question: Convert the binary number 10110110 to denary.
steps: Write the place values above the bits: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1
Add the place values wherever there is a 1: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2

blocks.question: Convert the denary number 217 to 8-bit binary.
steps: Start from the largest place value. Does 128 fit into 217? Yes → 1, leaving 89.

blocks.question: Convert the hexadecimal number B7 to binary.

blocks.title: Why hex?
blocks.text: The mark scheme wants: it is shorter than binary, so easier for people to read, write and remember, and less prone to error — and it converts easily because one hex digit is exactly four bits. Two of those points normally gets you two marks.
Binary addition works exactly like column addition, with only four rules to remember.

blocks.question: Add the 8-bit binary numbers 01101100 and 00110101.
steps: Work right to left, column by column, carrying where needed.

blocks.title: Overflow
blocks.text: If the answer needs a 9th bit but you only have 8, the carry out of the most significant bit is lost and the stored answer is wrong. That is an overflow error. Always say "the result requires more bits than are available" — that is the phrase the mark scheme is looking for.

blocks.title: The precision point
blocks.text: A right shift question worth 2 marks almost always wants the second mark for noticing that bits shifted off the end are lost, so the answer can be less accurate than a true division.
A character set is an agreed list of characters, each with a unique binary code. Without a shared standard, text sent from one computer would be gibberish on another.

rows: English letters, digits, punctuation, control codes
Every writing system in the world, plus emoji
Larger for the same English text

blocks.title: The rule that gets asked
blocks.text: n bits can represent 2ⁿ different characters. So 7 bits gives 128, and 8 bits gives 256. Expect to be asked this directly.
One useful fact: in ASCII the letters are in order, so if "A" is 65 then "B" is 66. The lower-case letters start at 97, which is exactly 32 more than the upper-case ones.
A bitmap image is a grid of pixels. Each pixel's colour is stored as a binary number, and the number of bits used per pixel is the colour depth.

items: Resolution — the number of pixels, e.g. 1920 × 1080. More pixels means more detail and a larger file.
Colour depth — bits per pixel. 1 bit gives 2 colours; 8 bits gives 256; 24 bits gives over 16 million.
Metadata — the extra information stored with the image (width, height, colour depth, file type) needed to reconstruct it.

blocks.title: Image file size
blocks.text: File size in bits = width × height × colour depth. Then ÷ 8 for bytes, ÷ 1000 for kB, ÷ 1000 again for MB. Write down every division — the method marks are there even if the arithmetic slips.

blocks.question: An image is 1024 × 768 with a colour depth of 24 bits. Calculate the file size in MB.

blocks.text: Sound is analogue — a continuous wave. To store it digitally the computer samples it: measuring the amplitude at regular intervals and storing each measurement as a binary number.

items: Sample rate — how many samples per second, measured in Hz. Higher rate means a closer match to the original wave.
Bit depth — bits per sample. Higher bit depth means each measurement is more precise.
Duration — how long the recording lasts.

blocks.question: A 2 minute stereo recording is sampled at 48,000 Hz with a bit depth of 24. Calculate the file size in MB.

blocks.title: Watch the units in the question
blocks.text: Minutes must be converted to seconds. Stereo doubles the size. And check whether the question says 1 kB = 1000 bytes or 1024 — it will tell you, and the answer changes.

keyTerms.definition: A base-2 number system using only 0 and 1, matching the two states a circuit can be in.
A base-16 number system using 0–9 then A–F, used as a shorthand for binary.
When the result of a calculation needs more bits than are available, so the answer stored is incorrect.
keyTerms.examWording: the result requires more bits than are available, so the carry from the most significant bit is lost

keyTerms.definition: Moving all the bits left or right, which multiplies or divides the number by a power of 2.
An agreed list of characters, each with a unique binary code.
keyTerms.examWording: a defined list of characters recognised by the computer hardware and software

keyTerms.definition: The number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel.
The number of pixels in an image, usually given as width × height.
Data about the file, stored alongside it, needed to interpret the file correctly.
The number of samples taken per second when recording sound, measured in hertz.
The number of bits used to store each sound sample.

examTips: Write the place values 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 at the top of the page before you start any binary question. It costs five seconds and prevents most errors.
Always check a binary conversion by converting back the other way. It takes ten seconds and catches almost every slip.
On file size calculations, show every division on its own line. Method marks survive an arithmetic error; a bare wrong answer earns nothing.
For hex to binary, go via nibbles, never via denary. It is faster and there is less to get wrong.
commonMistakes: Getting the place values backwards. The 128 is on the left.
Forgetting to divide bits by 8 to get bytes.
Forgetting that a stereo sound file is twice the size of a mono one.
Saying overflow is "when the number is too big" without saying it needs more bits than are available.
Giving a right-shift answer as a decimal. Binary shifts discard the lost bits — 9 right-shifted by 2 is 2, not 2.25.

title: Boolean logic
summary: Three gates — AND, OR, NOT — and the truth tables that describe them. This is a small topic with predictable questions, which makes it one of the cheapest sets of marks on Paper 2. Get it fully secure and it stays secure.

blocks.text: A logic gate takes one or more binary inputs and produces a single binary output. J277 requires three of them.

blocks.svg:

blocks.caption: The three logic gates required for J277, with their standard symbols.

blocks.title: Remembering which is which
blocks.text: AND is strict — everything must be true. OR is generous — one is enough. The AND gate symbol has a flat back like a capital D; the OR gate is curved.
A truth table lists every possible combination of inputs and the output for each. With n inputs there are 2ⁿ rows — 2 inputs gives 4 rows, 3 inputs gives 8, 4 inputs gives 16.

blocks.title: Never miss a row
blocks.text: List the input combinations by counting up in binary: 00, 01, 10, 11. For three inputs: 000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111. Do it that way every time and you will never duplicate or skip a row.

blocks.question: Complete a truth table for the expression NOT (A AND B).
steps: Set up columns: A, B, A AND B, then NOT (A AND B).
Fill A and B by counting in binary: 00, 01, 10, 11.
Work out A AND B for each row: 0, 0, 0, 1.
Invert each of those for the final column: 1, 1, 1, 0.
blocks.answer: Output column: 1, 1, 1, 0 — it is 0 only when both inputs are 1.

blocks.title: Add a working column
blocks.text: For any expression with brackets, add a column for the bracketed part first, then use it to work out the final column. It is faster, and if you slip you still pick up the working mark.

Exam questions usually give you a real-world scenario and ask for the Boolean expression. The trick is to translate the English literally, one clause at a time, and use brackets to keep the grouping right.

blocks.question: A greenhouse fan (F) turns on if the temperature is high (T) AND either the window is closed (W) OR the door is closed (D). Write the expression.
steps: Find the outermost operator — here it is the AND joining "temperature is high" to the rest.
Work out the bracketed part: window closed OR door closed → W ∨ D.

blocks.title: Brackets are worth marks
blocks.text: T ∧ W ∨ D is not the same expression as T ∧ (W ∨ D), and it will not be given the mark. If the English has an "either … or" inside a bigger condition, that part goes in brackets.

blocks.caption: The same logic written as a condition in code.

keyTerms.definition: An electronic component that takes binary inputs and produces a binary output according to a fixed rule.
Output is 1 only when all inputs are 1.
keyTerms.examWording: output is true only if both inputs are true

keyTerms.definition: Output is 1 when at least one input is 1.
keyTerms.examWording: output is true if either input is true

keyTerms.definition: Output is the inverse of the input.
A table listing every possible combination of inputs and the resulting output.
A statement combining inputs with AND, OR and NOT that evaluates to true or false.

examTips: Count up in binary when filling the input columns. It guarantees you get every combination exactly once.
Add an intermediate column for anything in brackets — it is faster and it earns working marks.
When translating English into an expression, deal with the bracketed "either … or" part first, then join it on.
This topic reliably appears on Paper 2 for 3–5 marks. It is small enough to master completely.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that a 3-input truth table needs 8 rows, not 6.
Omitting brackets, which changes the meaning of the expression.
Mixing up the AND and OR gate symbols. AND has the flat back.
Reading "either A or B" as exclusive. In J277, OR means at least one — including both.

title: Computational thinking
summary: Three principles that sound obvious and are not: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking. The exam does not want the definitions on their own — it wants them applied to a problem you have never seen. This topic also covers structure diagrams, which are drawn, not written, and lose marks for very predictable reasons.

blocks.text: Abstraction means removing or hiding detail that is not needed, so that only what matters is left. The word doing the work in that sentence is NEEDED — and what counts as unnecessary depends entirely on the purpose.

blocks.text: The Tube map throws away real distances, real directions and every street above ground. For "which train do I take and where do I change?" none of that matters, and removing it makes the map far easier to read. For "how far is it to walk?" the same map is useless. Same territory, different purpose, different abstraction.

blocks.title: Abstraction is not "simplifying"
blocks.text: It is not summarising and it is not making something easier. It is removing detail that is not needed FOR A PURPOSE. If you cannot name the purpose you cannot judge the abstraction — so in an exam answer, always say what it is for.

rows: Roughly what the sky will do
Deciding at a glance whether to take a coat
Where each player starts and who covers whom
The pitch, the ball, everything that happens after kick-off
Which room and which subject, by period
What is taught, who else is in the class, the walk between rooms
Getting to the right room at the right time

blocks.text: Decomposition means breaking a large problem into smaller sub-problems, each of which can be solved on its own. You keep going until each piece is small enough to solve easily.

items: Each small problem is easier to understand and solve than the whole thing.
Different people can work on different sub-problems at the same time.
Each part can be tested on its own, so a bug is far easier to locate.
A sub-problem solved once can often be reused in another program.

blocks.title: Two marks means two benefits
blocks.text: "Give two benefits of decomposing a problem" is a standard 2-mark question. Pick two from the list above and make them separate points — "it is easier" said twice is one mark.
Algorithmic thinking means working out the exact steps, in the right order, that solve a problem — and that would solve it again with different inputs.

The test of an algorithm is that someone, or something, could follow it without making a single judgement call of their own. "Play a good move" is not an algorithm. "If the centre square is empty, take it; otherwise take a free corner" is.

blocks.title: How to tell the three apart in a question
blocks.text: Abstraction — what did they leave out, and why? Decomposition — what did they break it into? Algorithmic thinking — what are the steps, in order? If a question asks about all three, answer it in that order and give each its own paragraph.
A structure diagram shows a decomposition as a picture: the whole problem in a box at the top, its sub-problems in boxes underneath, and their sub-problems underneath those.

blocks.caption: A vending machine decomposed to three levels. "Give change" is broken down further because it is the hardest of the four.

blocks.title: The three rules that earn or lose the marks

steps.title: One job per box
steps.text: If a box needs the word "and" to describe it, it is really two boxes.

steps.title: Every box joined to its parent
steps.text: A box floating on its own shows no structure, so it earns nothing.

steps.title: No arrows
steps.text: A structure diagram shows structure, not order. Arrows showing what happens first belong on a flowchart. This is the mistake examiners see most.

blocks.title: Structure diagram or flowchart?
blocks.text: Structure diagram: what the problem is made of, drawn as a tree, no arrows. Flowchart: the order steps happen in, drawn with arrows and standard symbols. Reading the question wrong here costs the whole answer.

sections.title: Applying all three to an unseen problem

blocks.text: The six-mark version of this question always gives you an unfamiliar program and asks how the three principles would be used to build it. It is marked on the application, not on the definitions — so name the principle in one clause and spend the rest of the sentence on this specific problem.

blocks.question: A student is writing a program to play a simple card game against the computer. Explain how they would use abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking when developing it. [6 marks]
steps: Abstraction — the program does not need the pictures on the cards, their thickness, or the sound they make. Each card can be reduced to a suit and a value, because that is all the rules use.
Abstraction, second mark — say the purpose. The detail kept is exactly what is needed to decide who wins a hand; everything else is removed because it plays no part in that.
Decomposition — the problem breaks into shuffling the deck, dealing hands, taking the player’s turn, deciding the computer’s move, comparing the cards, and keeping score.
Decomposition, second mark — each of those can be written and tested on its own, and "compare two cards" is reused every single hand.
Algorithmic thinking — the computer’s turn has to be an exact rule, not a judgement: for example, play the highest card of the suit led, and if you have none, play your lowest card.
Algorithmic thinking, second mark — the steps must be in a fixed order (deal, then play, then compare, then score) and must work for any hand the shuffle produces.
blocks.answer: Six marks, six points: two on each principle, each one applied to the card game rather than defined in the abstract.

blocks.title: The trap in every question of this type
blocks.text: Defining all three correctly and saying nothing about the problem in front of you scores about half. The examiner is checking whether you can use the ideas, not whether you memorised them.

keyTerms.definition: Removing or hiding detail that is not needed for a particular purpose, so only what matters remains.
keyTerms.examWording: removing unnecessary detail so that only what is needed for the purpose remains

keyTerms.definition: Breaking a large problem into smaller sub-problems that can each be solved on their own.
keyTerms.examWording: breaking a problem down into smaller sub-problems

keyTerms.definition: Working out the precise, ordered steps that solve a problem, and would solve it again with different inputs.
A set of precise, ordered steps that solves a problem or performs a task.
A diagram showing a problem at the top with its sub-problems branching below it. No arrows.
One part of a decomposed problem, small enough to be solved and tested on its own.

examTips: Always name the purpose when you write about abstraction. Without it, "removing unnecessary detail" is only half an answer, because nothing is unnecessary in the abstract.
On a 6-mark "explain how all three would be used" question, give two points per principle and apply every one of them to the problem in the question.
"Give two benefits" needs two genuinely different benefits, not the same one reworded.
If you are asked to complete a structure diagram, count the empty boxes — that is exactly how many sub-problems they want.
commonMistakes: Defining abstraction as "making something simpler" or "summarising it". It is removing detail that is not needed for a stated purpose.
Putting arrows on a structure diagram. Structure diagrams show structure; arrows show order and belong on a flowchart.
Writing boxes that do two jobs. If the label contains "and", split it.
Answering an "apply it to this problem" question with textbook definitions and no reference to the problem.
Mixing up decomposition and abstraction. Decomposition breaks a problem UP; abstraction strips detail OUT.

title: Programming fundamentals
summary: The first Python lessons, and the written-exam questions that come out of them. Paper 2 asks about this on paper, away from a computer — so you have to be able to state what a line of code outputs, spot an error in code somebody else wrote, and explain the difference between the two kinds of error, without being able to press Run.

rows: Where you TYPE your program. Nothing here runs until you press Run. This is what gets saved.
Where your program TALKS to you. Output appears here — and so do error messages.
Runs the saved file from the first line to the last.
An error message. Read the LAST line first: it names the problem. Then look at the line number.

blocks.title: The save rule, all year
blocks.text: Save the file BEFORE you type anything, and again before every run. Use surname_python1.py. Code typed straight into the shell is gone the moment you close it — and you cannot hand in what you cannot find.

blocks.title: Why this is an exam question, not just a lesson
blocks.text: "Explain one reason a programmer saves code in a file rather than typing it into the shell" is worth 2 marks. The answer: the file is saved permanently so it can be run, edited and tested again later, whereas anything typed into the shell is lost when it closes.
Anything inside quotation marks is printed exactly as written. Anything outside them, Python tries to work out. That single distinction is worth several marks a year.

blocks.code:
print(7 + 3)        # 10        — a calculation, so it is calculated
print("7 + 3")      # 7 + 3     — text, so it is printed as text
print("7" + "3")    # 73        — two pieces of text joined together
print("=" * 20)     # ==========…  — the string repeated 20 times
blocks.caption: The four cases you must be able to tell apart on paper

blocks.text: The last one is worth knowing for its own sake: "=" * 20 is better than typing twenty equals signs because the width is in one place. Change the 20 and every banner in the program changes with it, and you cannot miscount.

blocks.code:
# Python 1 — written by Harry
# Prints the menu header
print("Hello, Year 10")
blocks.caption: Comments explain WHY, for the humans who read the code later

blocks.title: What a comment is actually for
blocks.text: Python ignores comments completely, so they change nothing about how the program runs. They exist to make the program easier for a human to understand and maintain later — which is the wording the mark scheme wants.

rows: The code breaks the grammatical rules of the language, so it cannot be translated or run at all. A missing bracket or quotation mark.
Python tells you, with a line number
The code runs perfectly but produces the wrong output.
Nobody tells you — only testing finds these
The text has no quotation marks, so Python looks for a variable called Hello
Capital P — Python is case sensitive and the function is print

blocks.title: Both appear as written questions
blocks.text: Paper 2 asks you to define these and to spot them in a code extract on paper. The tell: if the program will not run at all, it is a syntax error. If it runs and gives the wrong answer, it is a logic error.
A variable is a named location in memory whose value can change while the program runs. Assignment puts a value into it, and the equals sign means "becomes", not "is equal to".

blocks.code:
name = "Harry"          # assignment: name becomes "Harry"
age = 15
age = age + 1           # reads as: age becomes the old age plus one
print(f"{name} is {age}")

blocks.title: Constants
blocks.text: A constant is a named value that cannot change while the program runs — VAT rates, the number of players, a maximum. Using one means the value appears once and is named, so it cannot be mistyped in one place out of twenty.

keyTerms.definition: A named location in memory whose value can change while the program is running.
A named value that cannot change while the program is running.
Giving a variable a value. In code the equals sign means "becomes".
A line ignored by the computer, written to explain the code to a human reading it later.
keyTerms.examWording: makes the program easier for a human to understand and maintain

keyTerms.definition: Code that breaks the rules of the language, so it cannot be translated or run at all.
keyTerms.examWording: breaks the rules of the language so the program will not run

keyTerms.definition: Code that runs but produces the wrong output. Only testing finds these.
keyTerms.examWording: the program runs but gives an incorrect result

keyTerms.definition: The console where a program’s output and error messages appear. Nothing typed here is saved.

examTips: On "state the output" questions, look first at whether the thing is inside quotation marks. Inside means printed as text; outside means worked out.
When asked to correct a line of code, write out the whole corrected line, not just a description of the fix. The mark is usually one for identifying and one for correcting.
For a syntax-versus-logic-error question, the giveaway is whether the program runs at all.
Python is case sensitive. Print, PRINT and print are three different things, and only one of them exists.
commonMistakes: Saying a comment "makes the code work better". It changes nothing about how the program runs — it is there for the human reader.
Reading print("7" + "3") as 10. Both are strings, so they are joined: 73.
Calling a missing bracket a logic error. If it will not run, it is a syntax error.
Writing code in the shell and then having nothing to hand in.
